newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe gives civil servants 30 percent pay rise.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe gives civil servants 30 percent pay rise.

text.p: Zimbabwe has awarded civil servants a pay rise of at least 30 percent after negotiations between staff associations and the state, a cabinet minister said on Friday.

Public Service, Labour and Social Welfare Minister Florence Chitauro said in a statement the increases were effective from July 1 and would cost the government an extra Z$9.1 billion (U.S.$798.2 million) in the new 18-month financial year which started on July 1 and ends December 31, 1998.
On July 24, Zimbabwe will introduce an 18-month budget as a bridge to align the state financial year with the calendar year.

Chitauro said the 30 percent rise included a final 20 percent tranche of a 60 percent phased award made last year under a contentious job evaluation exercise which led thousands of civil servants to go on strike to press the government, among other demands, to give them the total 60 percent pay increase.

She said public servants would receive other benefits including performance awards to be paid in November and December this year and next year, which would cost the government over Z$2.1 billion (U.S.$184.2 million).

"Whereas the agreement resulting in the wage increases awarded was achieved within funds approved by government for purposes of salaries and allowances increases in the next 18 months, it is crucial that wage increases are synchronised with the ability to pay, and the impact of the size of the expenditures on the overall economy," Chitauro said.

Public spending in the financial year ended on June 30, at 37 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) -- down slightly from the previous year's 40 percent -- remains well above levels recommended by the International Monetary Fund and other key Western donors bankrolling the country's economic reforms.

Chitauro said the government's persistent borrowing from the domestic market to finance its budget deficit, expected to widen to 11 percent of GDP from a target of 8.9 percent, threatened macro-economic stability and sustained economic growth.

The government of President Robert Mugabe has been under pressure from the Western donors to scale down high borrowing from the domestic market, which is seen as crowding out the productive private sector.

The donors, led by the World Bank and IMF, have withheld crucial balance-of-payments support for the past two years after the government failed to meet some key economic targets, including bringing down its budget deficit.
